strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 15 scenes with in-scene, out-of-scene, and cross-dataset generalization studies, including detailed ablations that identify important features (FoV counter dominates for full-scene depth UE)
Consistent and significant empirical improvements over FisherRF baseline, with AUSE improvements of 75.8-78.3 percentage points and Pearson correlations up to 0.85 for object-centric depth error

Practical post-processing approach that operates without modifying GS training, with novel demonstration of moderate out-of-scene generalization for UE in GS—addressing a previously underexplored aspect
Clear and well-structured presentation with effective visualizations (Figures 1-2) and extensive supplementary material enabling reproducibility

Valuable feature importance analysis demonstrating that most uncertainty maps carry meaningful information and identifying actionable insights (e.g., visibility-based features outperform error-based features for depth UE)
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: individual components (visibility/error aggregation, gradient boosting, von Mises-Fisher distributions) are standard; the contribution is primarily in their combination rather than in fundamental advances

Method requires ground truth hold-out views for regression training, significantly limiting applicability in real-world scenarios with sparse or unverified data; the claim of 'uncertainty without holdout data' in the abstract is misleading

Direction-dependent features provide only marginal or detrimental benefits (helpful on LF, harmful on TUM object-centric evaluation), adding complexity without consistent gains, and lack clear analysis of when/why direction-dependency helps

Evaluation limited to object-centric scenes from two similar datasets (both indoor/controlled); no evaluation on diverse capture patterns, dynamic scenes, or multiple outdoor scenes—generalization to torch (outdoor) scene completely fails

Rendering error UE substantially more challenging than depth error with significantly lower full-scene correlations (0.217-0.321 vs. 0.635-0.715 on TUM), suggesting method's universality is limited; particularly weak cross-dataset generalization for rendering error

Modest cross-dataset generalization with significant performance drops (e.g., LF-trained depth model on TUM: 0.139 correlation); negative correlations common in multi-scene settings; object-centric generalization substantially better than full-scene, indicating limited robustness
Limited baseline comparisons: only FisherRF (2023) evaluated despite recent concurrent work [1, 6] (2025); no comparison with ensemble, Bayesian, or NeRF-based approaches
Hyperparameter choices lack justification: von Mises-Fisher κ=8 and SH degree=4 selected without ablation; visibility thresholds not justified; no sensitivity analysis for number of hold-out views

No computational cost analysis despite rendering 13+ feature maps; missing analysis of why error-based features rank poorly; CNN spatial interaction results presented without deep analysis of asymmetric benefits across error types

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing an important gap in uncertainty estimation for Gaussian Splatting
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with extensive ablations and multiple evaluation settings (in-scene, out-of-scene, object-centric)
Informative step-wise backward regression analysis identifying which uncertainty features are most informative
Demonstrates partial out-of-scene generalization capability, distinguishing from baselines
Clear presentation with extensive supplementary materials and detailed experimental tables
Explores both depth and rendering error estimation systematically
weaknesses: Misleading claims about eliminating holdout data requirement—only applies to weak out-of-scene generalization; in-scene UE still requires holdout views, a significant practical limitation
Moderate and inconsistent empirical improvements: AUSE improvements are often modest, rendering UE gains are weak, and performance varies substantially between LF and TUM datasets
Limited technical novelty: core components (visibility/error projection, FoV counting, von Mises-Fisher modeling, gradient boosting) are straightforward applications of existing techniques
Fundamental contradiction: error-based feature maps rank very low in importance, undermining the core premise that error projections are valuable; FoV counter alone captures most signal
Incomplete baseline comparisons: only compares against FisherRF variants; missing comparisons with concurrent work [6] on view-dependent UE and other recent GS uncertainty methods
Weak out-of-scene generalization: cannot generalize to outdoor scenes, performance drops substantially on unseen scenes (moderate 0.3-0.5 correlations), limiting practical utility
Post-processing only approach cannot improve GS reconstructions or guide training/active view selection, significantly limiting impact
Inconsistent performance across datasets: direction-dependent features hurt TUM while helping LF; different optimal configurations needed, suggesting dataset-dependency
Missing computational cost analysis and timing comparisons; important for practical deployment assessment
CNN experiments show spatial context provides minimal benefit, suggesting features lack robust spatial structure

strengths: Novel primitive-based representation approach for capturing error and visibility information, differentiating from prior parameter-based methods
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with extensive ablation studies, in-scene and out-of-scene generalization analysis, and detailed documentation in appendices
Consistent empirical improvements over FisherRF baseline across most metrics (up to 75.8% AUSE improvement) and high correlations with true errors, especially on foreground objects
Practical post-processing approach that does not require modifying Gaussian Splatting training, enabling application to any existing GS model
First to demonstrate out-of-scene generalization for uncertainty estimation models, showing the method captures scene-independent patterns
Insightful feature selection study via step-wise backward regression effectively identifying important uncertainty features (FoV counter primacy)
Well-written manuscript with clear methodology, good visualizations, and logical presentation of results
weaknesses: Limited evaluation scope with only 15 object-centric scenes (4 LF + 11 TUM SLAM) from controlled settings, raising concerns about generalizability to diverse real-world scenarios with complex geometry, occlusions, or dynamic content

Out-of-scene generalization substantially overstated: massive performance drops observed (LF depth: in-scene 0.78 → out-of-scene 0.13-0.17, a 83% drop), contradicting claims of moderate cross-scene capability
Fundamental dependence on hold-out views with ground truth labels severely limits practical applicability in scenarios where accurate depth/rendering ground truth is expensive or unavailable

Direction-dependent features inconsistently beneficial (help on LF, hurt on TUM object-centric), adding complexity without clear justification; von Mises-Fisher modeling appears over-engineered for marginal gains

Limited baseline comparisons with only FisherRF evaluated; no comparison with other recent methods mentioned in related work (Aira et al. stochastic GS, Wilson et al. semantic splatting), limiting assessment of whether improvements stem from better features or regression approach

Regression model choices underexplored: only gradient boosting and linear regression tested; CNN experiments fail to improve performance with unexplained analysis; gradient boosting hyperparameters and optimality not justified

Evaluation metric justification weak: Pearson correlation chosen as primary metric despite limitations; sometimes contradicts AUSE results (e.g., torch scene); R² rejection reasoning is unconvincing for regression task

Critical hyperparameter choices lack principled justification: κ=8 for von Mises-Fisher, spherical harmonics degree 4, visibility aggregation functions appear empirically driven without sensitivity analysis

Missing failure case analysis: poor generalization on torch (outdoor scene) acknowledged but not investigated; no discussion of method limitations for challenging scenarios (specularities, motion blur, occlusions)
Reproducibility concerns: code availability marked 'TBA'; gradient boosting implementation details absent; hyperparameter sensitivity unexplored; some design choices unexplained
Computational cost not analyzed: rendering 13 feature maps vs. 1 for FisherRF overhead not quantified; training time not discussed; practical timing comparisons missing
No statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests; with only 15 scenes, high variance likely but unmeasured; some reported differences marginal
Missing analysis on robustness to ground truth noise and guidance for practitioners on hold-out view requirements

strengths: Addresses important problem: uncertainty estimation for safety-critical GS applications with interpretable primitive-level representations
Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 4 datasets, rendering+depth UE, extensive ablations (scene separation, feature combinations, spatial interaction, generalization)
Strong empirical results on primary benchmarks, especially for foreground objects (AUSE <0.1, correlation >0.8), significantly outperforming FisherRF, manifold, var3DGS
Practical post-hoc method that doesn't modify GS training or degrade rendering quality (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS preserved)
Thorough supplementary material with detailed analysis of feature importance, cross-scene generalization, CNN spatial interaction, and qualitative examples
Demonstrates secondary benefit: direct use of uncertainty feature maps for active view selection, outperforming baselines
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core approach straightforward (project statistics onto primitives → render → apply standard gradient boosting regression); no fundamental insights into GS uncertainty
Practical constraint of holdout data requirement: requires per-scene regression training, limiting deployment flexibility and contradicting 'post-hoc' claim of full automaticity

Overstated generalization claims: Table 8 shows unreliable cross-scene generalization despite abstract/intro emphasis; rendering UE (entire scene) degrades significantly, only object-centric setting reliable
Handcrafted feature design with redundancy: 13 manually engineered features (Tables 4-5 show reduced sets maintain performance); no principled feature selection mechanism, undermining elegance

Experimental design fairness concerns: baseline FisherRF adapted with regression for scene separation study changing comparison; var3DGS uses stochastic GS variant with lower quality on LF; no statistical testing or confidence intervals despite single holdout view per scene

Incomplete failure analysis: no discussion of failure modes; background UE substantially worse than foreground (Table 7); large unexplained variance in generalization; missing guidance on applicability
Incomplete technical justification: gradient boosting hyperparameters unspecified, κ=8 choice unjustified, holdout view selection strategy undefined, no computational cost analysis

Presentation issues: dense writing with informal notation introduction; uncertainty maps difficult to interpret; key insights (feature importance) in tables without sufficient discussion; disconnect between AVS using coverage directly vs. learning full UE

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets with systematic ablations on feature combinations, regression models, and scene partitioning (foreground/background)
Consistent improvements over baselines (FisherRF, manifold, var3DGS) on AUSE and Pearson correlation metrics, with particularly strong results for depth UE
Interpretable primitive-level representations (FoV count, coverage, error statistics) with insightful analysis of feature importance via backward regression (Fig. 4)
Well-motivated practical problem (uncertainty estimation for safety-critical GS applications) and thorough documentation with extensive supplementary material
Demonstrates applicability to active view selection without requiring explicit regression model training
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: core contribution is hand-crafted feature engineering (13 statistics from training views) + standard gradient boosting regression; post-hoc design choices justified only through ablation rather than principled reasoning

Weak generalization to novel scenes undermines central claims: Appendix C shows ~60% performance drop when training on one dataset and evaluating on another (e.g., 0.192 vs. 0.509 Pearson correlation), making the 'generalization' claim overstated and limiting practical deployment without scene-specific holdout views

Persistent dependency on holdout data contradicts the 'post-hoc' framing: requires training regression models on 1-3 holdout views per scene, preventing truly scene-agnostic deployment despite claims of generalization capability

Modest empirical improvements with confounded comparisons: gains over FisherRF often marginal (direction-dependent features add ~0.005-0.010 AUSE); baselines use different GS training variants (stochastic vs. vanilla), making direct comparison unfair; AVS improvement is only 1.6% PSNR with unclear statistical significance

Critical lack of depth error definition and calibration analysis: 'depth error' relationship to geometric accuracy is unclear (ground truth derivation unexplained); no discussion of calibration (confidence → error rate relationship), which is essential for safety-critical applications

Object-centric setting shows method limitations rather than strengths: 3-4× better UE on foreground vs. entire scenes suggests the method exploits coverage patterns rather than learning robust uncertainty; requires Gaussian Grouping segmentation, reducing practical applicability

Design choices lack principled justification: 13 features appear arbitrary with significant redundancy (Tables 4-5 show only 6-9 needed); no principled feature selection methodology; hyperparameter sensitivity (κ=8, opacity threshold 1/255) unexplored; aggregation function choices (max/sum/mean) unmotivated

Missing key comparisons and analyses: no comparison with simpler baselines (multi-sample variance, ensembles); CNN experiments (Appendix E) show spatial context helps but are underexplored and disconnected; no failure case analysis; theoretical basis for feature design not articulated

strengths: Strong empirical results across multiple datasets with substantial improvements over baselines (AUSE, Pearson correlation) for both rendering and depth uncertainty estimation

Comprehensive experimental evaluation including extensive ablation studies (Fig. 4, Tables 4-5), scene separation analysis showing strong object-centric performance (<0.1 AUSE), and out-of-scene generalization analysis
Practical post-hoc method requiring no GS retraining, enabling broad deployment with minimal holdout data; effective for active view selection
Clear presentation with interpretable primitive-level representations, insightful feature importance analysis, and extensive supplementary material providing reproducibility details
Thorough scene separation study demonstrating particularly strong performance for foreground objects and providing insights into FoV/coverage feature importance
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: combines established techniques (statistic projection, feature map rendering, gradient boosting) without fundamental innovations; all 13 features are manually designed without learning representations

Overstated generalization claims: Table 8 shows significant performance drops for cross-scene training (e.g., depth on LF: 0.121→0.139 correlation). Authors acknowledge 'inconsistent depth scale across LF scenes' indicating scene-dependent behavior contradicting out-of-scene generalization claims

Regression model dependency without principled justification: requires holdout views for training; handcrafted feature set (13 features) selection process not well motivated; Tables 4-5 show full set typically needed per scene

Direction-dependent features provide only marginal benefits (small improvement for rendering UE, little effect for depth UE) while adding complexity, raising questions about cost-benefit justification

Missing computational analysis: no timing/efficiency measurements despite post-hoc claims; no statistical significance testing, error bars, or variance analysis across runs; hyperparameter selection (κ=8, SH degree 4) not justified
Active view selection underexplored: brief treatment, single dataset evaluation (MipNeRF360), marginal PSNR improvement over baseline (20.721 vs 20.392), simpler approach than main method
No failure case analysis: missing discussion of when/why method fails, which scene types are most challenging, or sensitivity to factors like sparse training data or extreme viewing angles

Incomplete evaluations: depth UE primarily on single dataset (LF); comparison fairness issues with stochastic methods (var3DGS, manifold) that modify GS vs post-hoc PRIMU; Tables 4-5 suggest potential overfitting to specific scenes
